guide_line: Closed changes keep the same mass, and one compound keeps one mass ratio.
steps: Dalton said each element is its own kind of atom. Atoms of different elements join in small whole-number ratios to make a compound.
Law of conservation of mass: a closed change does not make or destroy mass. Add the reactant masses to get the product mass.
Law of definite proportions: every sample of one compound has the same elements in the same mass ratio.
Law of multiple proportions: if two elements make more than one compound, fix the mass of one element. The masses of the other element are in a small whole-number ratio.

worked_example.q: In a closed flask, 12.00 g of carbon reacts with 32.00 g of oxygen and makes only one product. What mass of product forms?
steps: The flask is closed, so no mass enters or leaves.

similar_problem.q: In a closed flask, 8.000 g of sulfur reacts with 8.000 g of oxygen and makes only one product. What mass of product forms?
similar_problem.hint: Add the 8.000 g of sulfur to the 8.000 g of oxygen. Nothing else is in the flask.

problems.q: In a closed flask, 24.00 g of magnesium reacts with 16.00 g of oxygen and makes only one product. What mass of product forms?
problems.why: Mass is conserved in the closed flask. 24.00 g + 16.00 g = 40.00 g of product.
hints: Add 24.00 g of magnesium to 16.00 g of oxygen. The flask makes only that product.

problems.q: 15.00 g of compound A reacts with element B in a closed flask. The only product has mass 27.50 g. What mass of B reacted?
problems.why: Product mass equals A plus B. 27.50 g − 15.00 g = 12.50 g of B.
hints: Subtract the 15.00 g of compound A from the 27.50 g of product.

problems.q: A 10.00 g solid breaks down in an open dish. 6.000 g of solid is left, and the rest leaves as a gas. What mass of gas left?
problems.why: The missing mass is the gas. 10.00 g − 6.000 g = 4.000 g.
hints: Subtract the 6.000 g of leftover solid from the 10.00 g that started in the dish.

problems.q: Every sample of compound Z is 40.00% element Q by mass. What mass of Q is in 12.50 g of Z?
problems.why: Definite proportions keeps the percent fixed. 0.4000 × 12.50 g = 5.000 g of Q.

problems.q: A 20.00 g sample of compound W contains 8.000 g of element X. What mass of X is in 50.00 g of W?
hints: Element X is 8.000 g in every 20.00 g of W. Apply 8.000/20.00 to 50.00 g.

problems.q: A 4.000 g sample of a compound contains 1.500 g of iron. What mass of iron is in 10.00 g of the same compound?
hints: Iron is 1.500 g in every 4.000 g of this compound. Scale that fraction to 10.00 g.

problems.q: With 1.000 g of carbon, compound A contains 2.284 g of oxygen and compound B contains 4.568 g of oxygen. What is the ratio of the oxygen mass in B to the oxygen mass in A? Use 4 significant figures.
problems.why: Fix the carbon mass, then divide the oxygen masses. 4.568 g / 2.284 g = 2.000, a 2-to-1 ratio.
hints: Divide 4.568 g of oxygen by 2.284 g of oxygen. Leave the 1.000 g of carbon out of the division.

problems.q: With 2.000 g of element M, compound 1 contains 3.000 g of Q and compound 2 contains 9.000 g of Q. What is the ratio of the Q mass in compound 2 to the Q mass in compound 1? Use 4 significant figures.
problems.why: The mass of M is the same in both compounds. 9.000 g / 3.000 g = 3.000.
hints: Divide 9.000 g of Q by 3.000 g of Q. The 2.000 g of M is the same in both, so it is not the ratio.

problems.q: A sealed flask has mass 36.00 g before a reaction inside it and 36.00 g after. Which mass law is this?
problems.why: The flask is sealed and the mass does not change. That is the law of conservation of mass.
hints: The sealed flask stays 36.00 g. Name the law that says mass in a closed change does not change.

problems.q: Water from a river and water made in a lab both contain 8 g of oxygen for every 1 g of hydrogen. Which mass law is this?
problems.why: Both samples are the same compound and the oxygen-to-hydrogen mass ratio matches. That is the law of definite proportions.
hints: River water and lab-made water share one oxygen-to-hydrogen mass ratio. Name the law about one compound having one ratio.

problems.q: Carbon and oxygen form two compounds. For the same mass of carbon, the oxygen masses are in a 1-to-2 ratio. Which mass law is this?
problems.why: Two compounds of the same two elements give a small whole-number mass ratio. That is the law of multiple proportions.
hints: Two carbon-oxygen compounds give oxygen masses in a 1-to-2 ratio for the same carbon mass. Name the law about that whole-number ratio.

problems.q: A compound is 60.00% carbon by mass. In 25.00 g of the compound, what mass is not carbon?
hints: Find 60.00% of 25.00 g, then subtract that carbon mass from 25.00 g.
